I would like, ilr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, to make an observation in connection with the accident to the steamer [DOT] Grecian.' It seems that Captain Harrison, on coming in to Halifax harbour, availed himself of the services of a pilot. At the port of Halifax it is not compulsory on shipmasters to engage pilots, but they must pay pilotage ; and When a pilot is taken on board, the master of the vessel has the right to depend on him for the management of the ship. Captain Harrison engaged a pilot and gave him charge of the vessel. It is in evidence that he had some misgivings as to whether the pilot was conducting the steamer properly or not, and called his attention to certain matters in the course of navigation. But the pilot assured him that everything was all right, and the result was the ship was run on the rocks. An inquiry was held by a court presided over by Captain Spain. The result of the inquiry was that the court suspended the captain's certificate, apparently because the pilot did not take the ship safely into port, which, on the face of it, would appear to be a most outrageous judgment. The judgment was appealed from by Captain Harrison to the Admiralty Di-Mr. STEWART.
vision of the High Court of Justice in England. I wish to read a portion of the judgment, in order that the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries may see that Captain Harrison has been completely vindicated, and to impress on the hon. gentleman the necessity of doing something In order to secure a more suitable court for the trial of questions of this sort, in which the reputations and livings of honest and honourable men are at stake. The president of the court said :
It appears to be clear that there is no fault seriously to be found with the Master
Everything which was done was done by the advice and under the direction of the pilot himself, and I do not see how it could be otherwise. It is suggested that the captain might have gone and looked at the chart, which means that the captain should have taken charge of the ship. I cannot help thinking that the criticism which my learned brother expressed just now really sums up the whole case. The court below treated the matter as if the captain was in charge himself and as if there was not such advice available as that of the pilot. I confess I am quite unable to take that view. It appears to me that the captain was quite right in allowing the ship to be guided by the advice and under the direction of the pilot.
The judgment of the court goes on to explain that Captain Harrison was free from any blame of any kind in connection with tbe navigation of the ship, and that the first court made a mistake in supposing that the captain was responsible for bringing the ship safely into port and in suspending the certificate of the captain because the pilot was remiss in the performance of his duty. The point I wish to bring before the Minister of Marine is this. If the inquiry had been made by the court at the instance of the boat'd of trade in England and the captain exonerated, his costs would have been paid by the board. By parity of reasoning, he ought now to be reimbursed in some way the costs he has been subjected to in order to vindicate his character and recover his certificate, and I would ask the hon. minister to carefully consider the matter and see whether he cannot discover some way of reimbursing the captain for the very serious expenses to which he has been put, altogether apart from the injury done the reputation lie bore, which was a very high one indeed. I would also ask the hon. minister to consider whether some other tribunal might not be created more competent to weigh evidence and possessed of something besides merely technical marine knowledge.
I beg to move the adjournment of the House.

I shall examine into the matter and see what I can do.
Motion to adjourn withdrawn.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. R. Prefontaine).

speechtext: Has the hon. the Minister of Marine had any information from British Columbia regarding the fisheries ?

I have had no information from the head officer, who is away on the Quesnel spawning ground. He will be communicated with through Mr. Robinson, with whom I have been in communication since two or three days. I cannot do anything until I get a report from Mr. Sword, in view of the difference of opinion among those interested.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. It. Prefontaine).

speechtext: How many days is it since the first communication with the hon. minister ?

I do not remember exactly. The first communication, I think, was on Friday from the canners. I then telegraphed to Mr. Sword, and getting no answer I repeated the telegram. Mr. Robinson, his assistant, replied that Mr. Sword was at Quesnel, and it would take him two or three days to communicate with him. The answer of Mr. Robinson was to the effect that the fishermen differed entirely with the canners, and that the canners themselves were not unanimous, although the majority favoured the suggestion of closing the season. But until he got information from Mr. Sword there would be nothing done.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

I have received a copy of a communication sent by the Fraser River Canners' Association to the minister, in which they refer to what took place the other day. In it the secretary of the association, Mr. Burdis, says that he telegraphed the resolution which I read in the House the other day, to all the representatives of British Columbia. In reply he received a telegram from the hon. member for Westminster saying :
Wire received. Reports here say salmon running unprecedentedly.
To this telegram Mr. Burdis replied :
Positively worst run sockeyes ever experienced. Canneries closed down. Only 180,000 cases up to date. Not a fish has been spawned at Fraser river hatcheries. Unless fishing stopped none will get there and industry dangerously threatened. Please so inform the department and local members.
Mr. Burdis goes on to say :
This morning I was instructed to address the following telegram to the hon. Senator Temple-man:
Referring our wire yesterday. Salmon industry threatened with total extinction. Immediate action necessary. Absolutely no salmon on upper Fraser. Stopping fishing immediately ; only possible remedy. Urge government reply promptly.
The canners are now anxiously awaiting the
receipt of your decision in the premises, and sincerely hope, for the sake of every person concerned, that their request in this connection has been conceded.
Awaiting your esteemed consideration and reply.

So that the statement with regard to the falling off in the quantity of the fish cannot be disputed. It ought to be possible for the government to get information from its agents right on the ground, even if Mr. Sword is not there.

Before the Orders of the Day are called it is my great regret, to inform the House of .the death of one of our colleagues, in the person of Mr. Pierre R. Martineau, member for Montmagny, who departed this life yesterday. Mr. Martineau was- a man yet in the prime of life, having reached the age of only a little over forty years. As everybody knows who had the honour of his acquaintance, he had been in poor health for many years, and could perform his duties as a representative of the people only at the price of great personal suffering; which he bore with remarkable patience. His was a most gentle character, as every one knows who had the pleasure of coming in contact with him; and he leaves a memory as a public man which will be held in honour, while amongst his friends his life and character will always be remembered with appreciation. I know that I voice the sentiments of this House when I say that we tender to his family the sincere expression of our sympathy.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: I am sure that we on this side of the House fully concur in what has been said by the right lion. Premier. Thp praise he has bestowed on the memory of our late lamented friend is richly deserved. Mr. Martineau was to us all a great example. Ever since lie became a member of this House he has suffered from a painful disease, but in spite of it he performed his duties wonderfully well. He was a model in that respect. Although an invalid for so long, he was the perfection of courtesy, and those who had dealings with him always found him of even temper and saw him ever with a smile on bis face. To those who did not know Mr. Martineau as well as we do who live in the province of Quebec, I would say that he was known throughout the province as a lawyer of great talent and a man of deep convictions ; and when called upon to express those convictions he had all the eloquence Of sincerity. As I followed the remains of Mr. Martineau this morning, I felt, as we all feel, that the province of Quebec can ill afford to lose sucb men as our late lamented friend.

speakeroldname: Mr. GEO. AV. FOWLER (King's, N. B.).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to follow tbe example of some of tbe gentlemen who have preceded me and make an apology for speaking upon this question at this late stage of the debate. I do not think that any apology is necessary, for I believe that the discussion that has so far taken place on this most important and momentous question is but a short prelude to that wider and fuller discussion which must take place in the country, when, at last, hon. gentlemen opposite screw their courage to the sticking place, and dissolve the House and go to the country. I regret very much that my lack of familiarity with the language in which the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Behind) spoke last night will make it necessary for me to forego the pleasure of criticising his clever speech. I judge that it was a very clever speech from the enthusiasm with which it was received by his compatriots. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), was particularly enthusiastic in his applause, and, knowing that hon. gentleman's taste, I am satisfied that the speech must have been a very clever one to call forth such plaudits from him. As to the remarks of the hon. gentleman for Lisgar (Mr. Stewart), who spoke last, as he confined himself to a complaint of the freight congestion in his section of the country, and as that section of the country is close to the American boundary line, I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that .his best plan if he wishes that congestion relieved, is to support the scheme outlined by the leader of the opposition, rather than that of his own leader, as the government scheme will certainly not touch his section of the country.
Now, Sir, one of the arguments brought against the present scheme that we are discussing is the haste with which the measure has been brought down, that there was not time for due consideration, before this measure was submitted to the House and the country. But the reason given for this haste is that the country is to-day face to face with a crisis. The right hon. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir AVilfrid Laurier), in introducing this Bill alleged that the great danger which menaces Canada to-day is the abrogation by the United States of the bonding privilege. But is there any such danger, Mr. Speaker ? Is this not a mere bogey : a figment of the disordered imagination of a man whose brain has become less able to reason sanely ? AVe have had the so-called

privilege for many years, a privilege which lias been to an extent mutually advantageous to Canada and the United States. But, Sir, while we have reaped certain profits from it, is it not a fact that the United States have reaped infinitely greater advantages ? No man can adhere to the fact and say that the advantage is not greatly on the side of the United States. The Americans are a commercial people. In their foreign relations they are largely guided by a due consideration of what shall be best for themselves from a material point of view, and such being the case, there is no international complication in sight of so acute a nature as to render at all likely a recourse on their part to so harsh and unbusinesslike a measure as the abrogation of the bonding agreement between themselves and us. It has been urged that they might do this in order to inflict a loss upon us for some imaginary wrong which they might conceive we had inflicted upon them. The history of the relations between the two countries in the past if they should study It, and I greatly overrate the intelligence of American statesmen if they would not indulge in such research before taking so grave a step, would very shortly convince them of the utter futility of such a step as a means of destroying the commerce of this country. When the Dingley Bill was made law in the neighbouring republic, there were people who prophesied that a deadly blow had been struck at our trade, but the great test of time lias shown such prophesies and fears to have been unfounded. If the bonding privilege were abro- . gated, which country would be the greatest sufferer ? Not Canada. Mr. Speaker, but the United States. The seaport of Portland is practically maintained by the Canadian trade, which passes through it on its way to the markets of Europe. The Canadian export trade through Boston and New York also forms no inconsiderable part of the trade of these two great ocean ports; and the edict which would prevent Canadian goods intended for export abroad seeking an exit through these ports would destroy Portland, and seriously affect Boston and New York. It would be a political boomerang which would injure more the party setting It in motion than that against whom it was directed.
But, Sir, if our railways could no longer carry goods in bond for shipment through American ports would our produce of necessity remain unsold and decaying within our storehouses ? Have we now upon our own soil no railways for the carriage of freight froip the west to the east ? Have we not the Canadian Pacific Railway from Vancouver to Montreal, and tb" IotercoPnial to St. John and Halifax ? If the bonding privileges were taken away we are still in a position to do business at the old stand, and the foundations upon which our trade rests will have received no violent shock.

Indeed, as a matter of fact, we shall then be absolutely sure that the whole volume of Canadian trade will have its outlet through Canadian ports, instead of only a small part as at present. So, Sir, there are two very effective answers to the Premier's question with respect to the danger of the abrogation of the bonding privileges, one being that though the abrogation is, of course, possible, it is yet in view of the history of the past, of the circumstances of the present, and of the outlook for the future absolutely improbable, and the other that our present means of transportation upon our own soil by means of the Canadian Pacific, Canadian Northern, Canada Atlantic, Grand Trunk and Intercolonial Railways, are such that we could still carry our products at no greatly enhanced cost from the extreme west to our own eastern ports.
If the strength of a scheme should be judged by the strength of the arguments adduced to maintain it, and I submit this is a fair test to apply, and if this matter of the bonding privilege is a fair sample of the arguments in favour of this so-called transcontinental line, which terminates at one end in an inland city, then surely it is no abuse of language to say that a madder or more foolish national project was never devised by any government, however imbecile, in any country, however misgoverned. What could have been the object of the right lion, gentleman in bringing forward so absurd an argument ? The hon. gentleman, I understand, has made it a boast, or has at least on former occasions confessed, that he has a very imperfect knowledge of business, and I am sure, Sir, that after this he will find no one able to put so great a strain upon his conscience as out of mere politeness to contradict him upon the point. What, I say, could- 'have been his object in bringing forward so absurd an argument as that founded upon the wholly imaginary danger of the abrogation of the bonding privileges ? Well, Sir, I do not think the answer is far to seek. The right hon. gentleman knows full well, for he has on former occasions felt the force of it, the great strength of the national feeling of Canada, and he plays the unworthy part of endeavouring to stampede the people of this country to his absurd scheme by creating this abrogation bogey, and thus arousing the prejudices of the people and blinding them to the real nature of the Cox contract. Why, Sir, where is all the great friendship that he and his party have in days past professed for the great American nation ? Is this the only tangible result we are to have from that much heralded international conference, which we were told was going to smooth away forever any friction which had been created by the unwise policy of the Tory government toward our southern neighbours ?
We have been told, Sir, that this conference will shortly meet again. Will its '	321}
deliberations likely be assisted and a desirable end made more possible of attainment by reason of the Premier of Canada having solemnly declared in parliament that the nation with which he is endeavouring to treat on amicable terms, is subject to fits of frenzy and on occasion performs acts which if it were an individual would lead to confinement in a lunatic asylum ? And, Sir, in this connection behold the further marvel of that former staunch friend and admirer of American institutions, that hon. gentleman, who in his intense desire that friendship should be maintained by this country with the United States, advised retaliatory action on the part of the United States to force us into their arms, and who thereby did not earn the esteem of patriotic Canadians-behold, Sir, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) arising in his place and in the most pious and apparently heartfelt manner, solemnly saying ' Amen ' to all that his chief had said in depreciation of the American people. There is a French proverb which says under certain circumstances, 1 search for the woman.' Now, Sir, the venerable age and general reputation of the hon. member for North Norfolk would in his case render a search of that sort unnecessary, but neither would preclude us from looking for a motive for so sudden a volte-face. May it not he found, Sir, in the fact that the hon. gentleman realizes the administrative weakness and utter unfitness of some of the members of the cabinet from Ontario, and with characteristic modesty imagines that lie tS just the man for Galway, and so resolves, in a mad endeavour to gratify an ambition which has always been with him, but which he until lately saw no chance to gratify, to go back on all his former professions, forsake his 'American friends, and swallow, holus-bolus, a scheme which no longer ago than last May he most roundly denounced. Sir, if these hon. gentlemen, or if this government have information known to themselves alone that there is a real danger whether near or remote of the bonding agreement being abrogated by the United States, I submit it is their bounden duty to' give that information to the House and country, for, Sir, with what information is now before us, and under a fair and reasonable consideration of the circumstances, weighing the advantages reaped by the United States against the advantages enjoyed by Canada, no sensible man can honestly believe that there exists now the slightest probability of such abrogation. But, Sir, they do not give us such information, because they have no such information, and the spectre which has been raised is only a poor imitation ghost that would not frighten a school boy. Yet the Premier says if it were not for this question he would not bring this scheme before parliament, thus showing upon what a poor and baseless foundation this costly superstructure rests.

Another argument put forward to show the desirability of the railway scheme is that it will make possible the settlement of the northern part of Ontario and Quebec, and the central part of New Brunswick. It has been gravely asserted by bon. gentlemen whose ignorance of the subject is most profound that settlement in New Brunswick is confined to the coast line, and a narrow strip along the St. John river, and that the building of this railway to Moncton will open up a most valuable agricultural territory. One would think, Sir, to listen to these gentlemen that New Brunswick had only just been discovered and that the aboriginal Indian still roamed the wilds of that province, and the white man had not yet ventured out of sound of the sea waves. Sir, this gloomy picture of the condition of the settlement in New Brunswick is not borne out by the facts. It is true that we have some forest in that country, and, Sir, it is a valuable forest. It differs from the forests of Ontario inasmuch as it renews itself, if properly cut and managed, and is a most valuable asset of that province. It is true, Sir, that much of the land covered by the forest of which I speak, would make, if cleared, good farming land, but, Sir, while cleared farms with good buildings upon them can be bought for very little, if any more than the initial cost of the buildings, to say nothing of the improvements, and although such farms are situate close to school and church and neighbours, and all that goes to make life worth living, you will not find the young man of New Brunswick anxious to go into the green woods and do pioneer work in hewing out a farm from the forest, when to do so he has to separate himself from those social conditions which add pleasure and zest to life. And, Sir, in selecting the route through New Brunswick, the government have chosen one, which for the most part, lies through the most rugged, hilly and broken part of the whole province, a route that must be greatly lengthened, from the estimate given by the hon. gen-[DOT] tlemen supporting these resolutions by reason of the detours made necessary by the numerous hills, lakes and ravines which are found in that part of the country. A glance at the map will show that the route proposed follows what is practically the watershed dividing the streams flowing south-west from those flowing north-east and east, and the most casual observer will perceive what is the fact, that this is no route for a trunk road which is expected to be a competitor for the grain trade between the west and the east. That this is true is amply borne out by the reports of the engineer, Sir Sandford Fleming, who tried to get a central route through New Brunswick for the Intercolonial Railway which would satisfy the people of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and who finally reported in favour of the route by the valley of the Mr. FOWLER.
St. John and the shore route along the coast. The influence of Hon. Peter Mitchell and the Nova Scotia members backed by the advice of the imperial authorities, prevailed, and the Intercolonial Railway was built by its present route. There is one thing which certainly commends itself to any man who has travelled on the Intercolonial Railway from Campbeilton to Moncton, and that is its easy grades. Sir, I believe that by reason of the superiority of the grades on the Intercolonial Railway between Montreal and St. John over the grades on the Canadian Pacific Railway between the same points, and the superior condition of the road-bed of the Intercolonial Railway as well, freight, notwithstanding the considerably longer distance, can be hauled as cheaply by the Intercolonial Railway as by the Canadian Pacific Railway. There are upon a portion of the Intercolonial Railway from Campbeilton to Moncton, thirty-mile stretches of road of a dead level, and freight trains on that portion of the road can make faster time than express trains will ever be able to make over the Grand Trunk Railway, if it is ever built over the proposed central route.
In other parts of the Intercolonial Railway where there are heavy grades, a comparatively small expenditure of money will reduce them, and it has been estimated by competent engineers that a wery considerable shortening of the line of the present Intercolonial Railway could be made by a cut-off from Riviere du Loup to Matapedla, effecting a saving of at least sixty-five miles at a cost, on account of the character of the country there, not exceeding $2,000,000, and the grades upon the whole of the Intercolonial Railway could be reduced to a proper standard for not more than a $1,000,000 more. So, Sir, $3,000,000 expended on the Intercolonial Railway would give you a road, within at the outside limit, twenty-three miles as short as the best estimate you have of the proposed route and infinitely better as to gradients than the road upon which this reckless government, for the benefit of a few financiers, who wish to recoup themselves for the losses incurred by wild stock speculation, at the expense of the public, propose to expend a sum which at the lowest possible estimate will exceed $15,000,000 and will, when built, undoubtedly parallel the road now owned and operated by the government and upon which $70,000,000 of the money of this country has been expended. .
Now Sir, the Grand Trunk Pacific people did not ask for this eastern division in their original scheme presented to parliament at the opening of this session, nor would they accept it now if they had to build and finance it even with the same proportionate government guarantee, as they have in the case of the prairie section. But of course, if the government pays for the.

building of the road and gives them the chance under the guise of a construction company to make a few millions in the building, they would be extremely foolisli not to accept so generous a gift. If the government were really in earnest about getting the shortest route to an ocean port, they would follow the valley route to St. John and the course they have adopted shows that it is a political and not a commercial road they propose to build.
As to the character of the route from Quebec to Winnipeg. I am not in a position to speak with such certainty as, unfortunately owing to the lack of exploration and survey in tliat quarter, there is no data in existence, or at least, to which I can flud access, upon which I can base a just opinion. And this fact, Sir, is one of the grounds upon which I object to this project. Before the country is committed to a scheme which involves the building of 1,400 miles of railway, there should be positive information given to this House, and the country to show that the route selected is a feasible one, and that the railway, when constructed, can be made by reason of gradients and curvatures suitable for a great trunk road. Now, Sir, up to a few days ago, we had nothing but politicians' guesses for information with respect to that country. At length, however, we were given a glimpse behind the veil and were permitted to see where the Premier got the information which convinced him that that northern region beyond the height of land was really a modern Canaan, a land flowing with milk and honey, and only awaiting the hand of the husbandman to blossom into a veritable agricultural paradise.
An lion. MEMBER. Hear, hear.

Speaker, the hon. gentleman has been reading his speech from the commencement of it and the question which occurred to my mind was who had prepared it for him. 1 desire, as that hon. gentleman has called attention to me, Mr. Speaker, to call attention to the fact that the hon. gentleman is reading his speech.

I may say, Mr. Speaker, that if I have erred in that direction I have only followed the example of at least ninety per cent of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on that side of the House. Now, it seems to me

Air. Speaker, attention has been called to the fact that the hon. gentleman who is now addressing the House is reading his speech. I did not intend to call your attention to it or to raise the point of order, but the hon. gentleman having called attention to me, I desire to raise the point of order.
I call the attention of the hon. gentleman (Air. Fowler) to the fact that it is against the rules of the House to read a speech.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He is not reading his speech.

I have to take the word of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler). When the statement was made that he was reading his speech he said that some other hon. gentlemen had been reading their speeches. I am not aware whether some other hon. gentlemen have read their speeches or not, because if they have done so, my attention has not been icalled to the fact.
It is a pity that hon. gentlemen opposite did not all read their speeches.
-Since my attention has been called to it I must rule that it is against the rules of the House for an hon. member to read his speech.

I have no paper in my hand. I have notes before me, I do not wish to offend against the rules of the House nor do I know that I offend against the rules of the House when I refer to notes. It seems, Sir, that the hon. member for Renfrew (Air. Mackie) was the chosen vessel, that that hon. gentleman was the one who supplied the information which made the Premier determine upon his course. Weil, Sir, the member for Renfrew has told us upon what he grounded his opinion as to the fertility of that region. He told us that he had tramped over a hundred miles of the territory with a pack on his back, when the soil was covered with a coating of snow three feet deep. Well Sir, all I can say is that the hon. gentleman must have a keen agricultural instinct if he could so confidently pronounce upon the quality of soil and it's suitability for farming purposes under circumstances such as these. But Sir, lest I should do the hon. gentleman an injustice, I must say he went further and informed us that he had learned of some other five hundred miles of that region from those most trustworthy persons-the Indians. And, Sir, when this astounding statement was made in this House the other day, the hon. gentleman supporting the scheme applauded vociferously, and looked over at us upon this side as though to say-Now you see we did know all about the country, it was no leap in the dark-We had full and authentic information from a man who knew all about it for the Indians told him so. In the late unpleasantness in South Africa, our friends the Boers had a famous gun, situated upon Talana Hill which from its length they named ' Long Tom,' and of which they were very proud, and each time it was discharged against the British they rejoiced greatly, though the damage it wrought was not at any time of much, if any importance. So our friends

upon tlie other side, when they had let off their * Long Tom ' in the person of the hon. gentleman from Renfrew, were most jubilant in their rejoicing, though as in the case of the Boers, the result was only an explosion. Now Sir, that country may he all that is claimed for it by the hon. gentleman opposite or it may be exactly the reverse, but I say this, that so far as any authentic information about the matter is concerned, no man either in the House or country is in a position to know, and before a contract for the construction of the road out of the public funds Is made, fully complete and accurate information should have been obtained. If Sir, we are to judge of the hinterland by the character of the country north of Lake Superior, then several hundred miles of the route must lie in a very undesirable region indeed, though of course, it may be it has all the fertility claimed for it, but 1 submit that before we can believe it we must have a proper exploration and survey. No man can be more averse than myself to saying one word against the greatness of this conutry or against the fertility of any portion of this country nor do I believe that any hon. gentleman on this side of the House during the course of this debate has uttered one word of a depreciatory character of the country which is in remarkable contrast to the conduct of hon. gentlemen who now occupy positions on the other side of the House, and who, when the Canadian Pacific Railway scheme was proposed by their predecessors in office, from the highest to the lowest, derided the country, depreciated its resources and belittled its future. We have had nothing of that kind on this side of the House and I was astounded myself when the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) stood up in his place in the House last night and made the statement that, out of all the hon. gentlemen who at that time were in this House supporting the Liberal party, Mr. Blake was the only one who had spoken in a derogatory way of the character of the North-west Territories. He was perhaps the most notable example because ne was then at the head of the Liberal party, but there were many others who did the same thing at that time and we had the spectacle the other day of a man who was a relic of that time standing up and saying that every word uttered in condemnation and in criticism of the scheme was borne out by the facts. But there are others of the Liberal party in Canada who do not take the view that the Minister of Trade* and Commerce professes to take. The hon. Geo. W. Ross, Premier of Ontario, admitted in a public address, that the Liberal party of that day was entirely wrong, and he apologized to the country for the course that he personally had taken in that matter.
We object to this railway project of the government, as I say, because the country through which it will run has not been fully

explored and surveyed. True, the country west of Winnipeg across the fertile plains of Manitoba and the Territories and over the passes of the Rockies to Port Simpson, is to some extent known to civilization. A great portion of this country is unequalled in fertility by any other part of this great American continent. But what does the government propose to do with respect to this part of the road which can be cheaply constructed' through a fertile territory ? They do not propose to build it themselves. Oh, no, that would be the part of wisdom, and it would not do to injure the symmetrical folly of this scheme by even one wise touch. And so, Sir, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway are to build this part of the road and they are to be assisted in the building of it by a generous government guarantee of bonds. But, what is the excuse put forward for the building of 1,400 miles of this government road through a district entirely unsettled and uninhabited ? It is, that this land which is entirely unknown as to its resources and capabilities for supporting population, should be opened up for settlement. Sir, is our population so crowded at the present day in the known parts of Canada, that it is necessary to go to this enormous expense in order to relieve the congestion ? Look at the map of the Northwest Territories and see the infinitely small portion of settled country, as compared with the unsettled part of that great region, and you have your answer. Is the government so blinded by their folly as to imagine that the people of Canada are going to settle amidst the forests, and to hew out of the green wood homes for themselves, when these immense western pariries only await the prod of the plough to burst into harvests of golden grain. The thing is absurd. No sensible man would settle in that country, even though it should be as fertile as gentlemen opposite pretend, so long as he can get a prairie farm on equal terms.
And then, Sir, if you do not require this road for colonization ; for what purpose is it required ? Its sponsors say that it is necessary in order to relieve the present congestion of the traffic in the west. It is practically admitted by men of experience that, if this government project is ever gone on with, it will take ten years to complete and equip. What, in the meantime, becomes of the freight congestion in the west, if it really exists ? With that end in view, and recognizing this urgent need, the government have entered into a contract, and the Bill giving effect to that contract is now before this House for its consideration. Its terms are well known, they have been discussed for many days, but I may briefly state them thus :
The plan is to build a grand national transcontinental railroad from ocean to ocean, wholly on Canadian soil. The eastern portion of that road from the city of Moncton to the city of Winnipeg is to be built at the country's expense. When built it is to be leased to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company with a reservation to the government of equal rights to use it. If government ownership of railways is desirable we will have under this agreement 1,800 miles of additional Intercolonial railroad which the government of Canada may use as to them seems best. In addition to that you could run your Intercolonial trains if you saw fit to the waters of the Pacific ocean and back again. That in short is the scheme proposed by the government, the scheme that is now before this House for ratification. protest against what ? My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) and late colleague, for whom I have a lingering affection, addressed a public meeting the other day and he is reported as having said, that he blamed the government for their indecent haste in' this proposition. Unfortunately, I was ill, and had not the pleasure of hearing the hon. gentleman when he spoke in the House, but I read the next day, I think in the ' Journal,' that he made a. very good speech on the waterways, but had been non-committal on the raiiway project. But, if he is reported correctly in the ' Mail '-and I give him the benefit of the doubt, because the ' Mail ' did not always tell the truth about him- if he is reported correctly in the ' Mail,' as stating that we are proceeding with indecent haste, then I have a few facts to call to his attention. He has professed to be- and I shall give him credit for sincerity-he has professed to be the friend of the manufacturers ; he has professed to be in favour of the employment of artisans and the encouragement of the industries of Canada. Let me point out to him that this government scheme means the employment of thousands and tens of thousands of men, that it means armies of operatives and mechanics in the manufacturing industries of this country, not one of whom would be employed under the railway policy of the leader of the opposition ; and having pointed this out to him, let me ask him, where is the indecent haste in our propounding a scheme that I make bold to say will do more for the artisans and the mechanics and the manufacturing industries of Canada, than any possible changes in the tariff could do for them ? If a man who is In favour of Canadian industries and employment for Canadian mechanics votes against this proposition of the government, and if he then goes outside and talks about his love for the working men and the manufacturers, his utterances are the merest vapourings. Indecent haste forsooth, when the country is crying aloud for increased

transportation facilities, and when we are engaged in a work that cannot be completed before five years from now. Who will say what the condition of this country will be, and what the magnitude of its trade and commerce five years hence ? Indecent haste forsooth, in bringing a project before parliament and keeping parliament here to satisfactorily deal with it, because there is necessity for this work going on and going on immediately. It would be more like indecent haste if this government had undertaken at this session of -parliament a general revision of the tariff, which I admit must be undertaken from time to time. It would be more like indecent haste if we attempted to do that at this session, when we are watching the progress of events in the old country from which results may transpire that will require the remodelling of our tariff in order to meet conditions that if we can bring them about will redound to the benefit of the agriculturist, and of every man that has a stake in the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite told us that we should postpone this scheme in order to attend to the tariff. Does any one pretend to tell me that this railway project of the government will not mean the greatest boom to our manufacturing industries generally ? The hon. gentleman from Toronto (Mr. Osier) mentioned a list of articles that he says will be required in the construction of this road. He read them coupled with the statement that they would come in free of duty. He was told by the Minister of Finance, that they will not come in free of duty, but, nevertheless he gave us a list of these articles. I hope my hon. friend from St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) will listen, so that he will see the wide spread benefit that this railway will confer on the artisans and manufacturers of Canada. Here are the articles mentioned by the hon. member (Mr. Osier) :
Tents, camp equipment, provisions, flour, pork,

You see where the farmer is benefited here :
-tools, scrapers, ploughs, steam ploughs for unloading, picks, shovels, spades, sledges, axes, saws, hammers, nails, spikes, crow bars, rails, semaphores, signal lamps, electric supplies, telephone supplies, wheel-barrows, carts, wagons, harness, all kinds of rubber goods, bedding, clothing, in fact everything used in the construction of a railway or in keeping up its supplies during fifty years.
How far-reaching will not be the supply of these articles by the manufacturers of Canada. How much will their production not benefit the artisans of Canada ? And what are we to think of hon. gentlemen opposite who instead of voting for a scheme that will secure this development of the home trade, purpose to support that hybrid-within a hybrid-enfolded-in-a-hybrid scheme, submitted to the House by their leader. Go on.

But, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) did say, that if this contract passed there would not be a steel rail rolled in Canada for 50 years. That was a beautiful idea ; was it not ? Well, if we buy up roads that are already railed, I suppose we won't roll any rails for them any way.
Hear, hear.
I must not speak at too great length.
Go on.

I have only spoken of two of the bits of road that these gentlemen opposite are going to buy, and now as to the two gaps they are going to fill in. But what more does their proposition involve 1 They propose to build these gaps at a cost of I do not know how much-I put it down at $4,000,000-but I will not commit myself to figures. Let me call the attention of the House to the fact that since hon. gentlemen opposite have announced their scheme, not one of them- except the member for Bothwell, and he only did so partially-not one of them has pretended to tell what the carrying out of their scheme will cost the country ; while on the other hand, we have given them every estimate and every detail of our scheme, and we believe our estimates to be correct. Therefore, I have to speak in general terms. But I put down-and I think it will be found to be a low estimate- -$4,000,000 as the cost of building these two gaps. That is putting the section which they are to build between Scotia Junction and Sudbury, which is a rough country at $25,000 a mile, which is the estimate we put upon our road through that level north country. I am charging no more for building through that rocky and difficult country than through the other ; but we want fair argument in this matter-no exaggerated figures. The proposition of the government stands out in bold relief to this, as two is to one.
Then, the buying of the boats-I put a query to that, how much ? I cannot tell you, and they have not told us. Surely they have a right to tell us what, or something approaching what, they will cosit. Then, I put another interrogative to the opposition : How many millions will they spend in assisting the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway in improving their roads from Fort William to Winnipeg ? They have not told us how much. Taking public money to pay the ordinary navvies employed on these two roads to make them better-to secure what? Well, to secure running rights to the Intercolonial and the Grand Trunk over these roads; forgetting that we have been told by some of the highest authorities on the other side of the House -that that is simply

an impossibility-an unworkable scheme. You cannot do it ; but they are going to do it. They are not to own that road after they have expended their millions upon it ; but they are only to have the right to run their trains over it from Fort Wililam to Winnipeg. And all this for what ? t ask the question in all seriousness; all this expenditure, more, far more, than by any reasonable calculation will meet the cost of those 1.800 miles of railway that we will build and own-all for what ? Transportation facilities this country wants; that is its need, whether the roads are owned and run by the government or by companies. What the country wants is the cheapest transportation it can get, whether under government control or under private control. What are we going to get, I ask ? Not one additional mile of transportation facilities-not one. Does any one mean to tell me that the government of this country could manage the Canada Atlantic Railway, and carry more freight over it at less cost than is done under its present able management ? Why, that would be to belie every experience we have. You gain not one iota, then, in solving the transportation problem. Will those facilities which they propose to buy carry one bushel more grain because they are owned by the government than if owned by an independent company? To ask the question is to answer it. To buy that section of the Canadian Pacific Railway-G29 miles cut out of it-does not lay a single new rail or another track. It is the same track, the same accommodation, not enlarged one iota for that expense. Do the running rights, secured by the expenditure of millions, over the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway from Fort William to Winnipeg, add to the facilities of transportation ? Not one iota. You have expended your millions, but you have not increased your transportation facilities by one bushel of grain or one pound of freight. That is the scheme of my hon. friends opposite.
Now, I want to have a little quiet pleasantry with my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule). I had not the pleasure of hearing his whole speech; but I read an article in the ' Mail ' of August 29 upon it. I always supposed that the 'Mail' was a friend of the hon. member for East Grey, but I do not see why it should do him the unkindness of publishing this portion of his speech. Of course, delivered as it was in a thin House, and embalmed in ' Hansard,' there was not much chance of any one seeing it if the ' Mail ' had not given publication to such a statement as this. Referring to the Grand Trunk Pacific my hon. friend said:
What does this scheme mean to the province X represent ? Suppose \ve build the road and it is a success. Suppose it carries all the grain from the west to the east, and the stuff from the east to the west, what does that mean Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
to Onta.rio ? It means that in proportion, as you make that road a great success, you impoverish the transportation routes we have today. You take away the trade that comes today to our Georgian Bay ports in the east, and that comes from Port Arthur and the head of Lake Superior to the west. It takes away the earning powers of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canada Atlantic Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway. It reduces their earning powers to the same extent as you make this other line a success. You must do it at their expense.
He sees no hope of expansion in trade; anything that is done must be done at tlie. expense of other companies; there can be no new business. There will not be under their system, I grant you; but be was speaking of ours. Therefore, be is concerned for the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific. All right ; but let us not forget that the plan of our bon. friends is to extend the Intercolonial into Winnipeg. Well, 1 suppose, in the hon. gentleman's concern for the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway, be would run the Intercolonial trains empty backward and forward just to show that hie owned the road, or else we do the other roads some injury. Sorry as be is about our scheme, be fears that it is going through, and he becomes resigned. He says:
I am willing to abide by the results, but I have only sympathy for the poor rate-payers who are to-day being plunged into the dreadful abyss. They cannot see what is before them in the future, the thraldom of the yoke is imposed upon them, and chains are shackled around them which cannot be unfastened for the rest of their natural lives by virtue of the great policy which was introduced and upon the advent of which we all heard such an hysterical acclaim as was given when the right hon. leader of the government gave it to this House, to this country and to the world.
Well, my hon friend was sad ! I fear that the scheme is going through, and if it should interfere with the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway, and the Grand Trunk Railway, we cannot help it. The country must go ahead. We have no feeling against those companies. We have largely subsidized and aided the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway, and I am very glad that we have done so. We have done very much for them in the past, and what they want in the future, in the interests of the country, they will get, I have not the least doubt, from this party or any other party-hut no corporation in the country is greater than the country, and the interest of no corporation will be allowed to stand in the way of this parliament legislating for the good of the country in such direction as it may seem fit.
Let us resume our narrative. The opposition are only at Winnipeg yet. They are in there only by going over 432 miles which they do not own. But what about the bon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy). He pro-

poses to assist the Grand Trunk Railway to build on reasonable terms from Winnipeg to Edmonton. But in what manner and at what price ? Is this aid they are going to give to be in cash or a guarantee ol bonds ?

It is to be reasonable aid, The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS. Reasonable. I am glad my hon. friend is there. He approached the discussion of this subject with about as fair a mind as any hon. gentleman on the other side, and while I do not wish to obtrude in family affairs, or offer my advice where it is not solicited, still I would suggest, that if by any chance there should be a change of government and this policy of buying the Canadian Pacific Railway be carried out, I hope that my hon. friend will be Finance Minister, because he places the cost of that road at only $45,000 per mile, and will thus save the country a good deal of money. In what shape are we to give this guarantee ? WTe aid the company for that thousand-mile by guaranteteing their bonds. There is not a penny of cost to us. We simply guarantee their bonds. If they pay the interest-and no one doubts that they will not be able to do it-we will not be a cent out of pocket. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, which will lease our line from Winnipeg to Moncton, will have that line fed by the Grand Trunk Railway and by its own western traffic. There will therefore be trade and traffic to go over it. But who will there be to feed the Intercolonial Railway, which the hon. gentleman would bring to Winnipeg ? Will the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern Railway ? Certainly not. You run your Intercolonial Railway to 'Winnipeg and there you stand. But where are you going to get your freight ? Will the Canadian Pacific Railway hand it over to you ? Not at all, because they will use their own road. Will the Canadian Northern Railway ? Certainly not, because they have a road of their own to use. Where then are you going to get your freight ? You may ask, where do these other roads get it. Well, they gather it through the prairies. But you will be in Winnipeg going over a country which it traversed by three other roads. I am afraid that the hon. member from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) would arrange things in such a fashion that the Intercolonial Railway will be running up and down there for the fun of it. What is the use of talking of extending the Inter colonial Railway to Winnipeg, at the cost of millions or tens of millions-I shall not be extravagant and say hundreds of millions-and leaving it there ?
The hon. minister is prov ing that there is no necessity for a transcontinental line.

I am glad to see that my hon. friend cannot
weaken my argument any more than he has done, because their proposition seemed to me so ridiculous that I thought there must be some solution of it. Apparently, however, there is none. We are building a road, Mr. Speaker, to a new country. The government are going to open up 3,000 miles of new territory. We are going to have the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway develop our western prairies and establish their steamship lines on the Pacific ocean, thus making traffic for the railway. Here is the advantage of our system, and it is not too late yet for hon. gentlemen opposite to support it. I ask them again who is to feed their road, which they will be running at so heavy expense. There is no one. Their scheme will mean empty trains at an expenditure of tens of millions of dollars, which may run into the hund-Teds of millions. I am not pretending to give you figures because you can figure it out for yourselves.
What we propose in regard to the mountain section is this : At a cost of about $450,000 per year, for seven years, which, if we paid all at once, would be a little more than $3,000,000, but which is spread over seven years, making the burden very light, we get a road built from Edmonton to the Rockies and the Pacific coast. Then our payments ceases. Hon. gentlemen opposite propose to build the mountain road.
I am taking that road on their own calculation, 500 miles at $50,000 per mile. Therefore, I estimate precisely for them what 1 estimate for us. They would build that road, 500 miles, at a cost of $50,000 per mile, which on the basis of my other calculation, making $25,000,000, and give running rights to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway over it. They do not say that they reserve to themselves the right to run their own Intercolonial Railwav cars over it. I have failed to discover that. They should at any rate make provision, as we have done, that the Intercolonial Railway trains may run over It.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me ? The Minister of Finance calculated it 480 miles at $40,000 per mile.
I made no calculation at $40,000 per mile. I made a calculation at the limit established by the contract, which is $30,000 per mile, and which is the extent of our obligation.

My hon. friend marred a somewhat able speech by a habit he has of just catching up a little difference like that, which should not come into consideration when you are talking about miles where there is not final survey or estimate. What is the use of talking about the difference between 480 miles or 450 miles or 550 miles ? What difference does that make in my argument, when I take precisely the same basis of calculating

the cost under their scheme that I do under ours ? That is not a criticism worthy of the hon. gentleman, and he would do better to try and keep on a higher plane. He is going to build that road for, say $25,000,000. Then he will lease it, I suppose, to the Canadian Northern Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and if he can get to it, he will arrange I . suppose to have the Intercolonial trains run over it. But how are they going to get over the intervening 1,000 miles between that piece of road in the mountains and the road finishing at Winnipeg ? When they get to Winnipeg, they seem to be tired and to want to rest. But when they are rested a few years, they will try and find a practicable route across the prairies, and then reserve running rights over this mountain section. This is to come after a few years. Well, I suppose that after trains have stood in Winnipeg for a while, after the lapse of some years-hon. gentlemen opposite do not tell us how many-our western farmers will have a chance to have some grain taken out by this government road. This will be a colonization road, a much cheaper road than we are going to build from Moncton to Winnipeg. They say it is to be built after some years, and will be built as a colonization road, I suppose with its light rails, sharp curves and heavy grades-and this is the road that is to afford relief to our farmers and prevent congestion of traffic. What a bonanza ? How the lands will increase in value in that country' when it is known what is proposed ! But, after they have had this colonization road running a thousand miles over the prairie,they are to build a piece of transcontinental road, a better road. Never mind paralleling and destroying the Intercolonial-they tell us they will build a better road than the Intercolonial Railway, from Levis to Moncton. But how will that dove-tail in with this colonization road from L6vis to the Rocky mountains ? This little one-horse railway will come down with its light engines and its few cars on a train and hand over the traffic to the road at Levis, to be taken over this road the cost of which we have estimated at $10,000,000, while they say $15,000,000-though that makes no difference, because, no matter what it costs us, they are going to make a better road than the Intercolonial, and it must therefore cost about the same as ours. So you have this fine road from Levis east to Moncton, and you have this colonization road trundling down its cars from the prairie country. I suppose that your road from Levis eastward with its heavy engines, its straight road and fine gradients, which will haul three times os many cars as the colonization road which is built to feed it, will run only one train in three days in order to allow for the second-class facilities of the other road. But ^ at least, with their plan, such as it is, these hon. gentlemen will have reached from ocean to ocean.

What then ? Under our contract we secure magnificent ocean fleets on the Pacific and magnificent ocean fleets on the Atlantic. We secure for the man in the west, as for the man in any part of this Dominion, a great working system which will be able to cope with an export rate from any far distant point in the North-west through to Liverpool and invaluable advantage to the people in cheapening through transportation. But under this scheme of hon. gentlemen opposite, where is your traffic ? And where are your fleets V You may provide this little line, but that is not developing the North-west, that is not providing the transportation facilities that are needed by the people of the prairies, that is not enhancing the value of the lands there. You must be prepared to quote as low rates as the other roads quote or you cannot get the export trade. So, you must consider the cost of your fleets, I will not attempt an estimate; I leave that for hon. gentlemen opposite. This is their scheme, and they are bound to give us some figures, some detail with reference to their plan. The government's plan is there, in black and white, duly signed-signed by men of repute, signed by the ablest railway men in the world, 1 believe. These men are not mere promoters. Mr. Charles M. Hays was-declared by the hon. member for Bast York (Mr. Maclean) two years ago to be the ablest railway man on the continent. Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson is known; Mr. Wainwright is known; Mr. John Bell, of Belleville, is known. These are the men who have signed that contract, and under that contract there is to be provided a line from ocean to ocean with its steamers on the Pacific to trade with the Orient, with its steamers on the Atlantic to carry the products of our western fields and of all portions of the Dominion to the furthermost nations on earth. That is what our scheme means. And as against this, hon. gentlemen opposite propose to build grain elevators at the country's expense to save the farmers of the North-west from building a hundred thousand barns. Why, the farmers of the North-west are not here asking for charity; they are not here asking the country to build the barns for them. Building elevators at the country's expense 1 Where will you get the grain to put in them ? You cannot get it on the prairies with such a road as is proposed by them ; you cannot get it at Winnipeg, for the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern Railway will not give it to you, hut will haul the grain to the head of the lakes or down to the Atlantic seaboard as the case may be and store it in their own elevators. I am afraid it will not work. The farmers will have to build their own barns, unless hon. gentlemen opposite can propose something better than this. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what does their whole scheme mean, this scheme which is to be carried out at the expense of untold millions-what

does it mean of actual accomplishment in the way of providing increased transportation facilities Nothing will be accomplished by it that cannot and is not accomplished better and more cheaply by the scheme proposed by the government. More than one of the hon. gentlemen opposite have told us that the congestion in the west is not due to there not being sufficient railway tracks, but to there not being sufficient rolling stock. Then let the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway buy more rolling stock and more locomotives. And in doing so either they wall buy them in Canada and so give employment to our own men, or they will import them from foreign countries, in which case the Customs Department would see to it that the revenue derivable therefrom is duly placed in the public exchequer.
But, Mr. Speaker, let us turn from the consideration of such a scheme as this and take a dispassionate view of the contract before us, this contract providing for the construction of a grand national transcontinental railway to meet the growing wants, and develop the resources of this country.
But before we do that, let me just for one moment allude to the objections raised by hon. gentlemen opposite. Nearly all, if not all of these objections, have been removed by their own plan. We heard a great deal at the start about paralleling the Intercolonial and destroying it by building from I-evis to Moncton, but their plan destroyed that argument. They said that our road is a hybrid system-but theirs is more. They said you could not give running rights to other companies, that that plan would not work, and yet they propose to buy a section and give the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway and the Intercolonial Railway running rights over it. But under our scheme they said you could not do it, you could not operate with running rights. Our proposition means an enormous addition to the debt, they say. Well, theirs means more. That I think is evident from what I have already said. They are going to do everything we had proposed except that they are going to build this as a colonization road in the north, saving perhaps $5,000 or $10,000 a mile on its construction, and in addition elevators are to be built, other roads are to be bought, and fleets are to be acquired on the lakes. Therefore, I think the less we hear from hon. gentlemen opposite about the expense of this contract the easier it will be for them in the time to come, when we have to debate this question in the presence of a larger audience, when the electors of this country shall be assembled, when the time comes for which some hon. gentlemen opposite profess to be anxious, and we appear before the electors to debate this subject with them. Let me tell them we are ready for that time whether it come early or come late, and, let there be no mistake, this subject will be discussed. No matter how our friends opposite may try to shirk it, we will see that they are held to it.
You cannot bring it on too quickly.

Too quickly 1 My hon. friend does not seem to be in a hurry for it, because he is moving a dilatory motion.
I have said that there was need of a grand transcontinental road. This country does riot want any such scheme as the opposition are talking about. The hon. members themselves are ashamed of it, they have not defended it in this House, aird I have noticed that their newspapers as a rule, do not defend the project as a whole. There have been one or two editorials-I read the ' Mail ' and the ' World ' regularly, although, of course, I take the antidote in the ' Globe ' and other papers in which I place more reliance-but the Conservative papers have scarcely had an editorial on the proposition of the hon. leader of the opposition. They have not had editorials on the whole of this scheme, but they profess to quote from the Montreal ' Witness' from the ' Journal ' of Ottawa and from the ' News.' The hon. senior member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), has not yet spoken ; like myself, I suppose, he has not had an opportunity. 1 have to bear testimony that our American neighbours in every matter connected with the bonding arrangements and wherever we have asked for an additional port, have courteously conceded it, as we on our part have done the same. I must say that the utmost good feeling prevails in that respect. But I tell you, that when Andrew Carnegie or any man of standing undertakes to write as an American citizen to such an influential journal as the London ' Times,' and endeavours to spread the belief in the minds of the English people, that if the 'bonding privilege were withdrawn we could not ship our grain to England, then, Sir, I must recognize the fact that Canada does well to provide by other means an additional outlet for her products. Let me point out that there is a good deal of trade coming to us through American channels.
The imports into Canada for the fiscal year 1902 were $212,270,158. The imports purchased from the United States were $129,801,847, and therefore the total imports purchased from all countries other than the United States amounted to $82,468,311.
Now, of that amount, $22,313,751 of our imports from foreign countries other than the United States, came through United States ports to us ; while $60,154,560 came through our own ports.
And now as to exports. The total exports of domestic produce in 1902 amounted to $196,019,703, and the exports sold to the United States amounted to $66,567,784. The value of exports of domestic produce sold to foreign countries other than the United States therefore was $129,451,979. The value of merchandise exported to foreign countries through the United States was $48,192,850 ; and the value of merchandise exported to foreign countries through our own ports was $81,259,129.
I give you these figures so that you may see that that is a large shipment of both imports and exports through the United States to or from Canada. If that privilege were withdrawn-and as I said before, I do not believe it will-it could not be without inflicting injury upon the United States, but nevertheless, when I find American citizens, for the purpose of trying to prevent Canadian farmers getting some cents a bushel more for their grain, using that argument,' fallacious though it may be, I believe in taking any strength there may be in such argument out of it, and providing another means for our products reaching other countries. I do not lose sight of the fact that our fertile plains are filling up, that our own sons have gone in there strong, sturdy and true Canadians, with the love of Canada in their hearts; and thousands and thousands have come to us from the United Kingdom, and we welcome them- they come with a strong British feeling in their hearts to make the very best of Canadians. But there are also large numbers coming from foreign countries and settling

there. They come without that strong feeling of Canadian nationhood that the others possess, but they will. I believe, become good citizens, and loyal to this Canada of ours, I believe, Sir, that nothing should be left undone to give satisfaction to the people who come to dwell with us, and with the intention of being fellow-citizens of ours in this country.
Should such an event happen as the doing away with the bonding privilege, we can stand it. Canadians cannot be coerced. The United States would suffer, but we would suffer too, for this reason, that though we have our outlet to the sea at all seasons of the year, yet, with the volume of trade that now comes to us through American ports, crowded in upon the trade that comes through our own ports, you would have a blockade in this country that would entail most serious loss on all our shippers and producers. Fancy all the exports of this growing country, in a few years from now, forced on one line of railway to find their outlet for five months of the year, and you would have congestion, delay and discontent arising in the minds of those whom we ought to take every means to make loyal, contented and happy. I believe in this expenditure to make us absolutely independent and unharmed, even if the United States should see fit to do away with the bonding privilege.
This railway will give the farmers of Manitoba and the North-west Territories railway competition, with its accompanying tendency of reduction in freight rates. 1 look for lower rates of freight through competition. It meets an imperative demand on the part of western Canada for better transportation facilities. Millions have been lost to the farmers in past years in consequence of the lack of facilities to transport the grain to market quickly; and in that remark I can only 'emphasize what I said before, that the opposition policy will not give one iota of relief in that direction. It will help to build up our Atlantic summer and winter ports; and fleets of steamships on both oceans will be provided without cost to us. It will give us another port on the Pacific, and thereby place us in a better position to compete for the trade of the Orient. It will attract immigration and capital. It will give a greater stimulus to the manufacturing industries of the country by enlarging the home market, to say nothing of the expenditure of money by the Grand Trunk Company and the government in the construction of the line. I need not go over that question; but you know that this company has to provide ,$20,000,000 worth of rolling stock, which will be made in the country if the factories are not crowded with work. But suppose that $10,000,000 worth of it is made in our own country and $10,000,000 worth is imported, because of our own factories not being able to keep up with the demand, you will have $3,500,000
of revenue from that. Then, consider all the men coming in, who will help to pay the revenue. I believe that the extra people to come into this country, necessitated by the building of this railway, and the additional development that it will produce in the country, will be such that by the time this railway is built and ready for operation, they will pay to the customs all that we shall have to pay during the seven years that the government will have to bear the interest on the cost of the road. When you consider the list of supplies that will have to come in, read by the hon. member from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) the other day, you can see how widely the influence of this enterprise will extend. It will give the manufacturers of Ontario and Quebec, now on the line of the Grand Trunk, an alternative line for the shipment of their goods to Manitoba and the North-west. Heretofore they have had to go to the North-west either over the Canadian Pacific Railway by North Bay or through American channels. This cannot but prove to be of advantage to these manufacturers.
Now, why should we not have the Grand Trunk in Manitoba and the North-west. I think my hon. friend from West Toronto favoured the Grand Trunk going into Manitoba. I think tbe hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) gave interviews in which he expressed the same view. Any business man in Ontario and Quebec knows what it means to him to have the Grand Trunk system extended into that country. You talk about the cost of carrying grain by rail. I do not go into that question. I believe a great deal of the grain will be carried by water; and the Grand Trunk will find its way to the water whenever it finds it necessary to do so. But while I love the North-west, I love the older provinces too, and we are not building this road simply to carry wheat out from the west. We want the older provinces to manufacture goods and send them up to the Northwest, where the people will buy them; and these goods do not go largely by water. I had myself some experience in business in days gone by, and no trifling difference in freight charges ever prevented me from shipping by rail. I wanted an all-rail shipment. I wanted to see the car loaded, and sealed through to its destination. That is the way a large part of the products of the older provinces will go to the west; and we want the Grand Trunk Railway, which has its ramifications in almost every village and town in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, to carry our manufactured products into that western country to be sold to our western brethren, ana to bring down their produce in exchange for them.
By building and owning the road from Moncton to Winnipeg, the government will hold' a lever which can be operated to the advantage of the producers in the west and

the manufacturers in the east. I have hastily run over the advantages of this contract. I have shown what we are to get. What are we to pay for this ? Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about $55,000,000. We expel id the money and build it, whether we pay $55,000,000 or $60,000,000, then we have the road, and at the end of the fifty years, when these bonds mature, they will have to be paid.
