I am sure the most enthusiastic admirer in this House of the speech to which we have just listened will not expect me to follow its ramifications in detail. Before the Minister of Customs took his seat, however, he made one statement to which I would like to reply. The hon. minister asked what possible prospect of success the Conservative party would have when next they appealed to the people of Canada upon the issues which separated the two parties if they went to the electorate bearing the banner of 'Little Canada'? I think, Mr. Speaker, that I can appeal to all fair minded men in this House and throughout Canada that if the banner of ' Little Canada,' if the policy of belittling Canada, if the policy of lack of confidence in the future of Canada, is borne or is presented

by any party in this country, it will be by the party of which the hon. gentleman is one of the leaders. The history of the policy of the two parties in Canada since confederation leaves no room for doubt on that score. The party which first of all united the several provinces into a confederation, the party which gave us the Intercolonial Railway, the party which gave us the Canadian Pacific Railway, extending from the western terminus of the Intercolonial Railway to the Pacific ocean, the party which built our canals, the party which made our water-ways navigable from the head of Lake Superior to the Atlantic-that party will never appeal to the people of Canada, and can never be made to appear to the people of Canada, as the Little Canada party. That party can appeal with confidence to the electors upon its past record and upon the platform which lias been laid down in this House during the last three years by its leader, and by the gentlemen who have the honour of supporting him.
The hon. minister in his opening remarks referred to the progress that is still being made and to the increase of imports into this country ; he referred with considerable pleasure and satisfaction to the fact that during the first two months of the present fiscal year the receipts from duties have increased by one million dollars as compared with the corresponding months of last, year, and he says the manufacturers of this country are so busy at the present time that they can fill only letter orders, that they have been obliged to call in their travellers because there is such a redundant prosperity in the country that they cannot accept all the orders that they might obtain. We can' congratulate the hon. gentleman on that happy condition of things, but we declare that the prosperity which obtains throughout Canada to-day is not by any means a result of any fiscal system that lion, gentlemen opposite may have improvised. It is rather the result of a series of abundant harvests which have blessed this country from end to end, and of the fact tl'at these lion, gentlemen ever since they attained to office have carefully avoided making any radical change in the fiscal policy Which they found on the statute-books when they came into office. The hon. gentleman says that as a result of the expansion which has taken place, and is taking place in this country, another transcontinental road is an absolute necessity. He says that we want additional facilities, and that under the plan presented to the House by the government these additional facilities are being abundantly provided. I was quite surprised to see the Minister of Customs rise in his place to take part in this debate, because if report spoke truly, if the statements that were being made about the corridors and in the House by those who are immediately associated witii 323i
the hon. gentleman and who are his political supporters were correct, no lion, gentleman on that side of the House was more opposed to the scheme which he has advocated to-day than was the hon. gentleman himself. What gave rise to his conversion ?
The circumstances under which the scheme we are considering was presented to the House were, to say the least, unusual. Parliament was called together on the 12th of March and in the speech from the Throne, placed in the mouth of His Excellency, we had a statement of the intention of the government to deal with this transportation question because, they declared :
The whole question of transportation and terminal facilities continues to occupy much attention, and my government will immediately appoint a commission of experienced men to report on the subject.
Later there was brought down a return to an Address of the House of Commons dated the 27tli of May, containing an abstract from the report of the committee of the hon. the Privy Council approved by the Governor General on the 19th of May, 1903, dealing with this very matter of making provision for the appointment of a commission to deal with this entire transportation question. Let me read again for the information of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House some of the paragraphs contained in this report of the Committee of the Privy Council to whom this matter was referred.
The minister submits that it may be assumed that grain and other products will naturally seek their markets by the cheapest routes and therefore the method to obtain the object desired should be to make the Canadian routes cheaper and more convenient than competing routes.
It would be an insult_ to the intelligence of the House and of the people of Canada to say that in anything that has fallen from the lips of the hon. gentleman who has just sat down, or in any argument which has been presented by hon. gentlemen opposite in support of the project "which we are considering, there has been the slightest scintilla of information given us as to how the desideratum mentioned by the minister is to be obtained by the government scheme. Has any hon. gentleman opposite attempted to prove, or in sincerity made the statement, that grain can be carried from the grain fields of the west to the Atlantic cheaper by this scheme than by the existing means of transportation ? Is there any person on the opposite side of the House who has had the hardihood to make that statement ? And yet. notwithstanding the fact, the incontrovertible fact, that grain is not carried by all-rail from the prairies of the west to the sea-board, the hon. gentleman and his associates in support of this proposition have declared that this grand transcontinental "railway is the solution of the transportation problem ; and he asks

the people of this country to endorse that proposition. The people of this country will do nothing of the kind, because they are convinced that the solution of the transportation problem, so far as it effects the congestion which occurs from time to time in j the western part of this country, can never be relieved by the construction of a national transcontinental line, involving the expenditure of one hundred million dollars or more, and laying a lasting burden of debt on the shoulders of the people of this country.
But let me read further from this memorandum :
The minister further states that the questions to be considered are complicated and involved, including among the objects to be sought the transportation of western products from place of production to the markets of the world.
What opportunity has been given to the hon. gentleman and his colleagues since this report was brought down or since this minute was adopted in council, to study this complicate and involved subject ? They have no more information to-day than was available on May 27th last, three months ago. And yet, notwithstanding the fact that they lack this information which is essential to a perfect, a sensible, an bonest, and a patriotic solution of this important question, they ask the members of this House and the people of this country to endorse a proposition to which they have given no consideration-for if they had given it consideration they cannot have given all the facts when this document from which I am quoting was brought down to the House. They have given it no consideration since then and they are in no better position to decide intelligently upon the question than they were three months ago when this return was brought down. I shall read another paragraph from this minute :
It is obvious that before any satisfactory conclusion can be reached upon these questions a thorough and comprehensive inquiry should be made.
Has a thorough and comprehensive inquiry been made since the 27th May last ? If so, who has made it 7 If it were essential before any satisfactory conclusion could be reached on the 27th May last that a comprehensive inquiry should be made, how can any bop. gentleman on the other side of the House stand up in his place and declare that this road fromi Winnipeg to the ocean supplies a satisfactory solution of a matter of so much importauce and one involving such a heavy obligation on the part of the people of this country ?
But the minute proceeds :
The minister further states that in making such investigation attention should not be confined to routes and facilities which are at present utilized, but, if necessary, new surveys should be made to determine whether any more economical and satisfactory channels of transportation by land or water can he opened up.

May I ask the Minister of Customs what new surveys have been made since the 27th May that have thrown additional light upon the subject and what additional information is in possession of the House ? Has the hon. Minister of Customs, or any one of his colleagues, any more information, the result of surveys that have been mpde, in their possession than they had on the 27th of May last ? Are they in any better position to state to-day what the possibilities of the new' country are than they were then ? Not the slightest. Yet notwithstanding the statements that were contained in this report to Council which was acted upon by the government we are asked to rush blindly into an expenditure of $100,000,000 for the construction of a road which will be of no practical advantage to tlie people ,and which will not relieve the congestion of the west which calls for relief as soon as it can be given. -
Further the minute states :
Diversion of Canadian products through eastern outlets to Boston. Portland and other United States ports, should he investigated, and the best and most economical method used by our competitors should be carefully studied and reported upon.
Has that been done ? Not a bit of it. Not a single report has been made, not a moment's investigation has been given to the diversion of Canadian trade through eastern outlets to Boston, Portland and other United States ports, and yet we are asked to go it blind and to accept the proposition which has been laid before us in the dying hours of this session and involve the country in tbe construction of tlie line from Moncton to Winnipeg which has never been asked for by the people of the maritime provinces, by the people of Quebec or of Ontario, and which is repudiated by the people of Manitoba.
The minute also states :
The minister further recommends that such scientific and professional assistance as the members of the commission may decide upon shall he employed.
What professional or scientific assistance has been called to the aid of the ministry to enable them to reach a conclusion such as that which they have presented to the House ? What information has been obtained by them since that report was made in May that places them in a better position than they were in then to advise the House and the country as to what course should be adopted to reach a satisfactory solution of this problem ? I would ask the lion. Minister of Customs if he has some light on this subject which he did not have then that has caused him to change his views and why he has become such "an ardent supporter of this scheme, which he looked at askance, during the last two or three weeks
Who told you that 7
A great many stories of that kind have been repeated from time to time.
Have there ?
I am sure there must be some foundation for them or they would not come from the quarters they came from.
Does the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) profess to deny the statement ?
Deny what ?	[DOT]
That he was opposed to this scheme at the outset ?
I am certainly in favour of it. I think I spoke in favour of it to-day.

This is not the first occasion upon which sudden conversions have been made. I would be very sorry to be in the position of doing the hon. Minister of Customs an injustice. It was current talk about the lobbies that the hon. minister was not in favour of the scheme of constructing another line from Moncton to Winnipeg and that he gave the scheme looks that were askance until quite recently. Does the hon. minister state that I am misrepresenting the position he took ?

I would like the hon. gentleman to state the source of his rumour. If the hon. gentleman is not able to give his authority then he must be responsible for it himself. Now, does he mean to say that I was opposed to this scheme ?
I have given the hon. gentleman an opportunity of denying the statement made again and again.
Make the charge.
And he has not availed himself of it. Now, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend the Minister of Customs
Let me say that while the hon. gentleman is not willing to assume the responsibility but to give currency to vague rumours that I deny the truth of the rumours which he says exist.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he denies having spoken against this proposition or having spoken disparagingly of it ?
That I have spoken disparagingly of it ?

Yes.
The MINISTER of CUSTOMS. Certainly, I deny it.
Of course, I must accept the statement of the hon. minister.
We are not dealing in rumours any more.

The hon. Minister of Customs called to time very harshly the Manufacturers' Association because of some action which they took that he thought was ill-advised. Action was taken because of the interpretation that has been placed upon clause 17 of the contract which hon. gentlemen opposite have made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The hon. gentleman thinks that the manufacturers have needlessly alarmed themselves, but if the clause had been worded as it should have been worded, and if the clause had not been so constructed as to give ground for the opinions which have been expressed on this side of the House the manufacturers would not have been alarmed ; but I am satisfied that the interpretation put upon the clause by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr.' Borden, Halifax), by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), who was buttressed by the opinion of one of the most eminent lawyers in this province, and by the opinion of" the hon. member for King's, N.B. (Mr. Fowler) who is an eminent lawyer in the province of New Brunswick, is the right interpretation, and that the interpretation that the hon. minister put upon it this afternoon is incorrect. The hon. gentleman said that partisan feelings must not be permitted to actuate the manufacturers. He Said that they must be absolutely non-political. Surely the hon. minister would not argue that if their construction of section 17 was correct, in a matter of so much importance to them, they were going out of their way in demanding at the earliest possible moment an explanation from the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as to the proper interpretation to be put upon this clause ? But when the hon. gentleman in a half threatening way referred to the manufacturers of this country I was reminded of the time a few years ago when some of his associates were coquetting with the manufacturers, were making pledges to them, not asking that they should abstain from any party political action, but, that they should do their best to help hon. gentlemen opposite in 1S96, and again in 1900, to secure a renewal of office from the .people. The hon. gentleman's colleagues and associates did not hesitate to promise to them an amelioration of their condition and an increased tariff if only they could secure the support of the manufacturers for the policy which hon. gentlemen opposite advocated.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

With the permission of .my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke), before he resumes his speech, I would like to state to the House that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has been confined to his bed through illness since last Friday evening. He has requested me to give notice of an amendment whicli he will move on the second reading of the resolution now under the consideration of the House, or, if he is unable to be present then, at the earliest possible opportunity. In view of what has been said by the Minister of Customs, I may say that this amendment had been prepared by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition for some days ; and he was only waiting a favourable opportunity to present it to this House. The amendment is as follows :
1.	That it is not expedient to ratify the agreement set forth in the schedule to the Bill now before this House entitled An Act respecting the Construction of a National Transcontinental Railway.
2.	That the government has failed to lay before the House such information as would justify parliament in committing the country to the agreement as a whole and especially to that portion of the agreement which provides for the construction of nearly nineteen hundred miles of railway constituting the eastern section of the railway therein mentioned.
3.	That the government in declaring its policy in the speech from the Throne at the opening of the present session gave a direct and specific pledge that it would immediately appoint a commission of experienced men to report on the whole question of transportation and terminal facilities.
4.	That in pursuance of this pledge the government on the 19th day of May, 1903, by an Order in Council touching the questions affecting transportation in Canada further declared its policy in the following words :-
The questions to be considered are complicated and involved, including among the objects to be sought the transportation of western products from place of production to the markets of the world.
This involves the consideration of their transportation :-
From place of production to Canadian seaports.
From place of production to the western ports to Lake Superior.
From the western ports of Lake Superior to Canadian seaports.
From Canadian seaports to Europe.
From place of production through Canadian ports on the Pacific.
As it affects the products of the eastern provinces of Canada it involves their movement:-
To the seaports.
From the seaports to Europe.
It is obvious that before any satisfactory conclusion can be reached upon these questions a thorough and comprehensive inquiry should be made regarding :-
The conditions of original shipment and the possibilities of improvement in the conditions surrounding such shipments.
The storage requirements of lake, river and ocean ports.

The harbour facilities of the inland lakes, rivers and Atlantic and Pacific ports.
The conditions with regard to the navigation of the St. Lawrence route, and, generally any improvement, enlargements, or other matters affecting the more economical and satisfactory uses of any Canadian channel of transportation by land or water.
In making any such investigation attention should not be confined to routes and facilities which are at present utilized but, if necessary, new surveys should be made to determine whether any more economical and satisfactory channels of transportation by land or water can be opened up.
The forces operating against the attainment of all Canadian transport, namely : -
Competition by United States railways ;
Competition by United States vessels from Lake Superior ports ; diversion of Canadian products through eastern outlets to Boston, Portland and other United States ports, should be investigated, and the best and most economical methods used Dy our competitors should be carefully studied and reported upon.
In these circumstances it involves upon the Dominion government to consider and adopt the best possible means of promoting such measures as may enable Canada to control the transportation of its own products, and it is thought that the most efficient method of conducting such an inquiry and obtaining the required information is by means of a commission of competent and experienced experts.
5.	That no such inquiry or investigation has been conducted or held and the ' required information ' referred to in the Order in Council above quoted has not been obtained or laid before this House.
6.	That this House is of opinion that the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway should continue to be owned and operated by the government of Canada.
7.	That the government system of railways should be developed and improved in the province of Quebec and in the maritime provinces and should also be extended from Montreal westward to such point or points as will enable it to transport to eastern Canada and to our national ports on the St. Lawrence and on the Atlantic the rapidly increasing products of our great western country.
8.	That by-
(a.) Developing and extending the government system of railways either by the construction of new lines, or sections of railway, or by acquiring and improving existing lines of railway ;
(b.) Securing under government control anl direction, or w'here expedient under government ownership, common haulage or running facilities in sections where one railway can usefully accommodate several systems :
(c.) Giving, if and w'here necessary, material aid by way of guarantee or otherwise, to rail-wav construction in the great west, and to colonization railways in the older provinces ;
(d.) Enlarging and improving our canal sys-em, developing our magnificent lake and river routes and thoroughly equipping our national ports on .the great lakes, the St. Lawrence and tho Atlantic seaboard ;
(e.) Perfecting a system of elevator warehousing, and creating free terminal facilities, and.
(f.) Securing absolute and thorough control of rates in consideration for assistance thus given.
We would open up new territories, provide for our products the best and cheapest trans-

port to the Atlantic and Pacific seaboards, connect without delay the great railway systems of the east and the west, relieve any threatened congestion of traffic and secure the transportation of our products through Canadian channels while at the same time we would stimulate and promote interprovincial trade between the various communities by whom the cost of such national undertakings must necessarily be mainly borne.
9.	That the management of government railways and of all railways under the control or direction of the government should be freed from party political control, influence and interference.
10.	That for the purpose of accomplishing these results the government in accordance with the policy wisely laid down in the Order in Council above recited, should avail itself of the best expert advice and assistance before seek ing to commit the country to expenditure upon any national transportation scheme or project.

I was very glad to give way to my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) so that lie might have an opportunity of presenting to this House the resolution which the leader of the opposition intends to move at the earliest possible moment. That resolution crystallizes the views and desires of lion, gentlemen on this side of tlie House as to an effective solution of this transportation problem. The resolution which has been presented is a most effective answer to the statement made by the Minister of Customs this afternoon as to the unwillingness of lion, gentlemen on this side to place themselves on record, and to present in some concrete form a counter proposition to that made by the government.
When you left the Chair at six o'clock, Sir. Speaker, I was pointing out that the Minister of Customs had lectured the manufacturers of Canada for exhibiting, as he said, party bias, in that they had asked for an interpretation of clause 17 of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway contract. The minister thought that the members of the Slanufacturers' Association were acting as political partisans, because, for the time being, they accepted the opinion presented from this side of the House as to the real meaning of clause 17, and as to the effect it would have upon the materials and supplies which would lie required, not only_ for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, but also for the betterment of the road during the 50 years it would be under lease. Let me point out to the Minister of Customs that the manufacturers took the only course they could legitimately take. It meant no disrespect to lion, gentlemen opposite, and in that view the remarks of the Minister of Customs were neither well-timed nor called for. The manufacturers of this country acted within their right. They had a perfect right to ask for an explanation at the earliest moment of the real meaning of clause 17. I repeat, Sir, what I said before you left tlie Chair at six o'clock, that if the necessary care had been taken in the drafting of that clause, and if it were less ambiguous than it is, then neither the manufacturers nor anybody else would have had any reasonable doubt in their minds as to what the true and real intent of that clause is.
But while with one breath the hou. Minister of Customs criticised the action of the manufacturers, charging them with being political partisans, and with acting in a partisan manner, in the very next breath he appealed to them that if they took any action or gave expression to any opinion respecting the project now before the House, they should have accepted the proposition of tlie government rather than that offered by tlie lion, leader of the opposition in the address which he made on this matter a few days ago. And what was the reason given by the hon. Minister of Customs why the manufacturers should accept tlie proposition of the government rather than that of the opposition ? The reason was, he said, that the government intended to build roads while the opposition intended to buy roads; or, in other words, that the proposition of tlie government involved an enormous expenditure of money, and that therefore tlie manufacturers of this country, whether they approved of that expenditure or not, should give the proposition which involved that expenditure their hearty support. The hon. minister was appealing to the selfishness shall I say-to the cupidity of the manufacturers; and he asked them to accept the scheme of the government rather than that of the opposition, no matter what effect that expenditure might have on the future of this country. Would it have been patriotic or wise or prudent on the part of tlie manufacturers of this country, or on the part of any other class of citizens, to approve of a proposition, merely because it involved a large expenditure of money, if they were not at the same time satisfied that the expenditure was judicious, and would result in permanent good to the country ? That was the principal reason given by the hon. minister why the manufacturers should have become partisan and should have accepted the proposition of the government. If, as we contend on this side of file House, the enormous expenditure which the government propose to incur is not warranted, if as we believe it is an unwise and foolish expenditure, notwithstanding the fact that that expenditure may for a time promote good times and give employment to a large number of people, the result will not be of permanent benefit to the country, but rather the reverse; for a reaction will take place, and the burden of tlie repayment of the large sum involved in .carrying out the government's proposition will rest on the shoulders of the manufacturers, the artisans and the farmers of this country, and will be a serious injury to them instead of being a permanent advantage. But, Sir, if the expenditure of a large sum of money is the only or the chief reason why tlie manufacturers and all other people

living in the Dominion of Canada should support the government scheme, may I not point out that if the Grand Trunk Railway had been permitted to carry out their scheme as it was originally presented to the people of Canada, the carrying out of that scheme would have involved the expenditure of a very large sum of money-a sum of money that would have been provided, not by pledging the credit of the people of Canada, not by adding largely to the burden of debt which now rests on the shoulders of the people of Canada, but by private enterprise-by tlie new Grand Trunk Company and those associated in the enterprise of extending their system into Manitoba and the North-west Territories. What was the tirst information the people of Canada received as to the intention of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to enlarge the sphere of their operations and to extend them into Manitoba and the North-west Territories ? The original proposition was different from the one we are now discuss1 ing in this important fact, that the present scheme involves practically the construction of another trunk line, duplicating the present Grand Trunk system from the city of Quebec to its western terminus in the province of Ontario, while the Grand Trunk scheme ns originally presented contemplated what ? Mr. Hays' declaration made in the city of Montreal on the 24th November was to the following effect:
This company is now prepared to go right ahead with a railroad extending from North Bay or Gravenhurst on our present line through that portion of northern Ontario, familiarly known as New Ontario, through Manitoba to either Bute Inlet or Port Simpson.
* The road will be of the most modern and up-to-date character for the handling of both freight and passenger business-in fact, the road will be of the highest standard in every respect.
No one who has been studying the wonderful developments that have taken place in the North-west during the past few years can fail to be deeply impressed with the growth of this extensive and rich territory ; and our directors feel that in view of the apparent need of additional railway facilities, and in order to guarantee the present Grand Trunk system, direct connection with that very important and growing section of Canada, the only wise policy is to take active steps towards this extension.
We are entrenched in the central portion of Ontario, the manufacturing district ; but when it comes to taking goods to the west, we only get the haul as far as North Bay. Under the circumstances, it has been felt that further development was necessary, and hence the present scheme.
That was the statement made by Mr. Hays, the general manager of the Grand Trunk system, a gentleman to whom my hon. friend the Minister of Customs paid a very high tribute because of his great executive ability and bis experience as the manager of a great railway system; in fact, the hon. gentleman looked upon him as possibly the ablest railway man on the con-Mr. CLARKE.
tinent of America. Mr. Hays was induced to enter into this scheme, not for the purpose of duplicating the Grand Trunk line for nearly 1,000 miles, but rather for the purpose of extending the present Grand Trunk system, which has its ramifications iu every industrial centre of Quebec and Ontario, from its western terminus at Gravenhurst or North Bay into Manitoba and the Territories-an altogether different proposition from that of the Prime Minister oil which this discussion is based. The opinion of Mr. Hays was buttressed by that of Mr. Morse, Vice-President of the Grand Trunk Railway, associated with Mr. Hays in the management of the Grand Trunk Railway. What did lie say ? At Winnipeg, interviewed by the correspondent of the Toronto ' Globe,' he said that they would begin at once; that there was to be no delay so far as the Grand Trunk was concerned ; that the work was to proceed as soon as they obtained legislation in this parliament to enable them to extend their system into Manitoba and the North-west.
We are going to build at once	What is
more important is the fact that we are not a new company. . . . Having connection through the best manufacturing districts in the east and to the Atlantic sea-board, that your people are most anxious to reach, you can see how it will benefit the west. On the one hand, is direct connection with manufactories that can supply the needs of houses in the west ; on the other is your direct line back to the sea-board. Of course, what we look to is the magnificent opportunity of opening up and developing one of the greatest stretches of country under heaven. I refer to that boundless tract of land which lies to the north-west of you.
The ' Canada Gazette ' corroborated exactly the views I have presented as emanating from Mr. Hays and Mr. Morse. The notice given in the ' Canada Gazette ' on the 20tli December last sought for incorporation for the new company-what for '! To extend the present Grand Trunk system from its present northern terminus at Gravenhurst or North Bay to Manitoba and the west; and the announcement made in the official organ of the government in the province of Ontario, the Toronto ' Globe,' reiterated and confirmed the opinions which I am now giving. The ' Globe ' said :
In view of the apparent need of additional railway facilities, and in order to guarantee to the present Grand Trunk system direct connection with that very important and growing section of Canada (the North-west), the only wise policy is to take active steps toward an extension in that direction which will be commenced as soon as the necessary legislation has been obtained from the government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask why the Grand Trunk Company were not permitted to proceed with their proposition ? What reason has been advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite why the scheme of the Grand Trunk Company was interfered with? They were prepared to proceed at once with

the construction of their railway to Manitoba and the territories, and they were prepared to proceed with that work without asking for more than the ordinary assistance which has been given from time to time by this parliament to railways in the various provinces to enable these railways to open up new portions of -the country.
I.ask why was the company forced to deprive the two principal provinces of the Dominion, Ontario and Quebec, of that direct connection with the territories ? The Grand Trunk Railway Company was prepared at once to proceed with the construction of that line. They would have built more than one thousand miles through that practically unknown territory where construction is most difficult, and they would have done that upon only the ordinary assistance or bonuses per mile from the government of this country. But what intervened ? What arose to prevent the construction of the proposed new line, which was to be an extension of the Grand Trunk Railway ? In March last, the government declared that they were going to have a commission to examine into the whole transportation business, but on the 30th of July last, they harnessed an impracticable allrail scheme on to a practicable rail and water scheme. That scheme involved the expenditure of a very large sum of money. The organ of the Liberal party in Ontario, the Toronto ' Globe,' estimated the expenditure at $100,000,000. The 'Globe' pointed out that that expenditure would mean a great deal for all parts of Canada, and undoubtedly it would ; but the ' Globe ' further said that it would not approve the expenditure of that very large sum unless it felt satisfied it would be a wise expenditure, and that those who invested their money in the enterprise would receive a reasonable return at once. This is what the ' Globe ' said :
_ The spending of $100,000,000 in the constructing ot the Grand Trunk Railway transcontinental system means much for all Canada. . . .'We should, however, deprecate the spending of such a vast sum. . . were we not absolutely convinced that the capital invested in the Grand Trunk Railway continental system, as Mr. Hays has outlined it, will pay handsome returns even before the road is built.
I believe that that statement is correct, and that had the Grand Trunk Railway Company been permitted to go on with its own scheme and g.et connection at the earliest possible moment with Manitoba and the territories, that scheme would have commended itself to the judgment of the people of Canada, and to capitalists outside of Canada, and the necessary money could easily have been raised to enable the Grand Trunk Railway to finance it; but for some inexplicable reason not given so far by any hon. gentleman opposite, the government, which in last March declared that this Whole transportation question was to be
referred to a commission, brought down on the 30th of July, after we had been five months in session, a new scheme which involved the construction of 1,800 miles of road by the government, and an expenditure anywhere from $80,000,000 to $100,000,000, and after the work had been constructed and that expenditure made, the whole railway was to be handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to operate during seven years without paying a farthing of interest, during three years longer without paying interest unless it earned it, and during the balance of the term of fifty years on paying three per cent interest on the cost of construction. I am utterly at a loss to understand why the government interfered in the proposition of the Grand Trunk Railway and insisted on building a road from Moncton to Winnipeg, and then handing it over to that company. It is a most extraordinary proposition, and the government have not yet made the explanations necessary to a proper understanding of a transaction of such vital importance.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister gave us some reasons with which I propose to deal at a later stage. But we have these facts patent:	The Grand Trunk Railway
were willing, of their own motion, to take the necessary steps to relieve any congestion that might exist in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and the government, instead of aiding the Grand Trunk Railway, are rather putting obstacles in their way. It is not argued strongly, to say the least, by hon. gentlemen opposite that the construction of a railway from Moncton to Winnipeg would relieve the congestion that exists in the North-west. It is not argued by any hon. gentleman opposite that relief can be given by the scheme before us in less than from six to ten years ; but that relief which the west demanded, the proposition of the Grand Trunk Railway in November last would give much more effectively and sooner than it can possibly be given by the proposition under consideration.
My hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) did my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island and myself, and some others the honour of quoting some statements which we made in the west, when up there last fall looking over that magnificent country. I am sure if what the hon. gentleman read to us this afternoon reflected the statements and sentiments to which we gave utterance during our visit to Manitoba, the North-west Territories and British Columbia, it may truthfully be said that we do not belong to the ' Little Canada ' party. We have as much faith in the future of that country as any hon. gentleman opposite can possibly have. And why should we not ? The party with which we are identified and associated is the party which, first in Canada appreciated the great

future of our country. It was the old chieftain who led that party in the olden days who proposed the legislation which procured for us that great western land and made it a part of this Dominion. It was the old chieftain and the Conservative party at his back who connected that great western country with the older provinces of the Dominion ; and notwithstanding the opposition offered by the right hon. gentleman's colleagues and himself, the great Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed at that time at the general expense of the people of Canada. Why ? Because of the abiding faith which the Conservative party had in the destinies of the country, because they were not afraid to pledge their faith by making large expenditures in order that that great North-west might be opened up and made easy of settlement to our kith and kin from across the Atlantic. We, therefore, would be belying the records of the Conservative party if, when we had the opportunity in company with our leader, whose absence we regret so much this evening, we did not reiterate those expressions of faitli and confidence and hope in the future which we- wer,e taught by the chieftains of the Conservative party in days gone by. But notwithstanding our optimistic views- -and I have seen no reason to change those views since I came back last November-I failed to see that there was any demand in that western country, or in any other part of the Dominion, 'for another transcontinental line, if I understand the meaning of that term. By transcontinental line, I mean a line extending from ocean to ocean ; and I make the statement, with the greatest possible respect for the Minister of Customs, that there was no demand from the west or the east or the centre of Canada for another transcontinental road such as we had described to us in such eloquent terms by my hon. friend this afternoon. What the people of the west wanted then, what they want now, is increased railway facilities, but that does not necessarily involve the construction of another transcontinental line extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific. What was being done when we were there last fall ? We found that railway development was proceeding apace. We found that the Mackenzie & Mann system was being extended east and west and north ; that the Canadian Pacific Railway was making great extensions to its system throughout Manitoba and the territories. We found railway development going on expeditiously with the objec t of relieving the congestion and providing for future development.
The government could not have contemplated, in March last, that this transcontinental railway was going on, for they certainly made no announcement of it. At the very least, they did not take the public into their confidence. My hon. friend' the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mu-Mr. CLARKE.
lock)-notwithstanding the fact that last March the hon. gentleman and his colleagues placed in the mouth of the Governor General a statement to the effect that this transportation question was to be referred to a commission for satisfactory solution-in speaking the other night, said : 'It took us a year to evolve our modest proposition.' Weil, I am bound to accept the statement of tlie hon. Postmaster General, made from his place in this House. But I must say that I cannot reconcile that statement with tlie statement made in the speech from the Throne or with the actions of the government since that sj>eecli was made on the 12th of March last. Was it the object of the government to deceive the country by putting these words into His Excellency's mouth ? I should hope not. If the government were working on this transportation scheme, if they thought that having an all-rail line from Moncton to the Pacific coast would be a solution of the difficulty, it was ridiculous to say that this was an involved and intricate matter, one that they could not deal with, and therefore proposed to appoint a commission to investigate and report upon. But this commission has not been given an opportunity to deal with it. And if the government have been working at this problem, working energetically and sedulously, for the last twelve months, what have they done? Are we to judge of their business capacity by what they have discovered and evolved in that twelve months ? What information have they laid before us as a result of their twelve months' labour? What have they done to demonstrate that they were working faithfully and zealously to solve this problem ? What business acumen have they displayed, after devoting twelve months to this question, in the scheme brought down to this House? They have not even a plan to present. They have no survey. They cannot tell us what the route of the proposed new line is to bo. We must take everything for granted. They tell us that they have mountains of information. Their information has not been disclosed by anything that they' have presented to the House; and if they have mountains of Information, they have kept it all to themselves. All the information vouchsafed to us is that presented by the right, hon Prime Minister, consisting of reports made by surveying parties who went up from the province of Ontario looking for timber, and also some musty reports taken out of the library.- The information contained in the reports of the Ontario surveyors is three years old, and the information contained in the reports from the library is twenty years old. The government might have obtained that information. not in twelve months, but in twenty-four hours, if they had decided to look for it. But, Sir, after twelve months' labour on tins scheme in endeavouring to evolve a solution of the transportation question,

tliey bring down to us a scheme without knowing witliin ten or even twenty millions what the carrying out of it will cost; without having the slightest idea of where the road is to run; without having the slightest information as to the character of country through which the road is to pass; without having the slightest information as to the engineering difficulties they will have to encounter before they can complete the work of constructing the road from east to west.
The Prime Minister has given us three reasons for the adoption of this scheme. And, if I have accurately read, and if I understand his speech, his reasons are : First, to jjrovide immediate means whereby the products of the west may find an exit to the east at the least possible cost; second, to provide a transcontinental line all on Canadian soil; and, third, for fear that the bonding privilege-* privilege,' mark you -should be taken from us by our American neighbours, and to be independent of them should such a contingency arise-in other words, to be prepared for the abrogation of that so-called privilege. These reasons of the Prime Minister are evidently given seriously. As to the first, the Grand Trunk itself would have provided for a speedier, cheaper and more direct solution of the problem than does this scheme presented by the Prime Minister. The Grand Trunk could have reached Manitoba and relieved the congestion there far sooner than can be done by the government's proposed line. The second reason, that we desire a transcontinental line every mile of it on Canadian territory, must have been given as a result of an oversight. Because, as I pointed out this afternoon, the people of Canada constructed the Intercolonial Railway from Halifax and Moncton to Montreal, and they also constructed the Canadian Pacific Railway from Montreal to Vancouver. So, while the right hon. gentleman was giving this as a reason, that, in order to be independent of our neighbours, we should have a transcontinental line every mile on Canadian territory, thanks to the patriotism, thanks to the willing sacrifices of the Canadian people to their national ideals, thanks to their desire to be independent commercially of the Americans, we have had just such a line in existence for the last ten or fifteen years.
Well, Sir. as to this bonding privilege. That was given as the third reason. It is said that we fear that the bonding privilege, so-called, might be abrogated, and therefore we must build this all-rail, all-Canadian line. Sir, we could and would have got along very comfortably for some years past, even if the bonding privilege had been abolished. And I think that, if it had been abolished, instead of being a source of ill and a source of loss to the country its.abolition would have redounded very substantially to the interest of the Intercolonial and for our maritime provinces. The bonding privilege is a venerable bugaboo, which has been made to do duty on many previous occasions. But it is a ghost that has been raised once too often. It was brought from its resting place on the occasion of the notorious Yukon deal. We were told, when that scheme was before us several years ago, that if we did not build that Yukon Railway, which hon. gentlemen opposite proposed, we should be deprived of the bonding privilege and our products would be shut out of the Yukon, or compelled to pay duty in crossing American territory. But parliament, on that occasion, did not take much stock in the argument that the bonding privilege might be abrogated, and the sending of our goods into the Yukon so interfered with. Parliament did not accept the proposition of the government. Notwithstanding that, the bonding privilege is exactly as it>
was regarding our goods going through Skag-way and other points to the Yukon, and all the way down along the border to the city of Portland, Maine. Why ? Simply because the Americans, our neighbours, are as much advantaged by the bonding privilege, aye, and more so, than are the Canadian people. That is the reason, and the only reason, why the bonding privilege has not been taken away from us. Well, Sir, my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) declared in his speecli this afternoon that the construction of this transcontinental railway will give immediate and permanent relief to Manitoba and the Northwest, and that it will be a substantial benefit to every province in the Dominion. I listened very attentively to what my hon. friend said respecting the advantages that the provinces of Quebec and Ontario would gain from the construction of this transcontinental road, and-I say it with the greatest possible respect-after the hon. gentleman had left that part of his argument, I felt that I was not much wiser than I had been before the hon. gentleman had spoken. The Grand Trunk proposition as originally made by that company would have placed every mile of the company's system in Quebec and Ontario in direct communication with its extension from North Bay. If the present transcontinental railway is built, what will be the result? The great centres of population, the great industrial centres, in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, will be separated by at least two hundred miles from the new transcontinental system; and if they desire to be placed in touch with that system, if they desire to get the advantage of passing the cars containing their products over that system, long branches will have to be constructed from Montreal, Toronto and other centres, in order that the manufacturers and mechanics of these provinces may be brought in touch with this transcontinental system and may derive advantage from the spending of money in its construction. Wliat is the position of Montreal, the great

industrial and commercial centre of Canada? It is the head of ocean navigation as well as the headquarters of the great railway corporations, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railways. It is the gateway of the St. Lawrence, it is the first distributing centre of the Dominion of Canada, it is the great monetary emporium of the Dominion of Canada, and in the construction of this line Montreal will be sidetracked unless a line more than 200 miles in length is constructed from Montreal northward to tap this new line on its way from Quebec city. The Grand Trunk Railway, in their original proposition, proposed to use the present Grand Trunk line from Montreal westward by the most direct line, and thus save the expense of handling and the great distance which will be lost by the adoption of the scheme proposed by the right hon. gentleman. Every industrial centre in the province of Quebec, except the old historical city of' Quebec and the industrial centres east of it, will be in exactly the same position as Montreal. The products of every industrial centre in Quebec will have to go by a roundabout way if this new road is to be used at all, to make connection with the new road 200 or 300 miles north of Montreal.
How is the great industrial province of Ontario to be benefited, how are its interests beneficially affected by the construction of this road ? The hon. gentleman who preceded me (Hon. Mr. Paterson) has not made this quite clear, and I hope that before the Bill passes its final stage he will give more definite and plainer information as to the benefit Ontario is sure to derive from the construction of this road. My hon. friend twitted the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) because they asked how Ontario was to be benefited by the construction of this road, and he tried to make it appear that they were sectional in their views because they did not at once swallow the scheme. Sir, the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway would mean an enormous expenditure in Ontario and Quebec. It would mean the expenditure of $25,000,000 in the province of Ontario ; and surely we who have the honour of representing that province in this House cannot be charged with being sectional because we object to the useless and unnecessary expenditure of $25,000,000 in that province ? We make that objection because we believe and feel that that expenditure is a useless expenditure and that the people of Ontario will have to pay their share of the debt imposed on this country by the construction of this line, but will derive no real, tangible or substantial benefit from it. For seven or eight months in the year, under present conditions, the industrial and commercial centres of Ontario have a cheaper and shorter connection with Mr. CLARKE.

Sir, this road will be 100 miles longer if tlie government's present scheme is insisted upon than the present all-rail communication with the west, or than the connection we can get, under the proposition made by the leader of the opposition, both by the Grand Trunk Railway and the Intercolonial Railway. would use this new route to send tlieir output to the west, when they have a hike and rail route 300 miles shorter. Now, one word about the Quebec section. The distance by the Canadian Pacific Railway from Montreal to Winnipeg is 1,424 miles, and by the Grand Trunk Pacific line it cannot be less than 1,475 or 1,500 miles. The Grand Trunk Railway has now 3,142 miles of track in Ontario and Quebec, and by the scheme proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition all of this great mileage is placed in immediate and direct communication with Winnipeg and with the west. Every mile of this 3,142 miles is dissociated by the proposition of the government from the new scheme, and will have to obtain access to the west if at all by th.e roundabout methods that I have indicated of connecting this system with the proposed new system. Sir, if the government had not imposed upon the country the obligation of building this line from Quebec to Winnipeg, what might have been done with the money it will cost ? The scheme which the leader of the opposition has presented to this House could have been, and would have been, fully carried out, if opportunity had been afforded him to do it. Access to Georgian bay and the west would have been obtained for the Intercolonial; the Grand Trunk would have got a right of way, a right of user, from its present north-western terminus over the Canadian Pacific Railway to Winnipeg ; the Mackenzie & Mann system, which now has its eastern terminus at Port Arthur, would have been brought down to Sudbury and Ontario. Then let us take the section of the route from Quebec to Moncton and see what is the situation. The government's proposal is for the construction of another line at a cost of $15,000,000. What will be the result of the expenditure of that vast sum of money ? What earthly good will it do ? It will not open up a tract of country of which very much use can be made in the way of settlement and agriculture ; and it may do a great deal of damage to the forests in that country. And what will be its effect on the Intercolonial ? AVe now have the Intercolonial from Moncton to Quebec, or Levis, which is just across the river ; and will the construction of this road be of any benefit to the Intercolonial ?
If the money that is to be expended upon the branch from Quebec to Moncton were saved to the country the present Intercolonial Railway might be shortened, if it could be profitably shortened, and every harbour on the Atlantic coast worthy the name as well as the harbours of Montreal and Quebec could be efficiently and properly equipped to do all the business that will offer for many years to come. The proposition of the government involves an expenditure of $15,000,000 to construct another line between Quebec and Moncton, when according to a statement made by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), and his statement has not been challenged by any hon. gentleman opposite, the Intercolonial Railway can now do four times the business that it is able to secure and do it satisfactorily and efficiently. I cannot for the life of me understand, and I have tried to give this matter the very best possible consideration, why the government is persisting and does persist in committing itself to this Quebec-Moncton branch. There is no demand from the maritime provinces for the construction of a trunk line through them. If it is necessary to have a new trunk line why not utilize the Intercolonial Railway from LOvis to Moncton arid include it in the scheme of a transcontinental road. As the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals pointed out, no better grades or as good grades can be found for any other road that will be shorter than the Intercolonial Railway, by the route which these hon. gentlemen propose to adopt ; and for this reason and for the reason that the Intercolonial Railway is only partially employed, while it is capable of doing a great deal more business, I cannot understand why the government will persist in committing the people of Canada to this needless, this unnecessary, this hurtful expenditure of $15,000,000, which might be put to much better use in making a more satisfactory solution of this transportation question than can possibly be made of it if the government persist in this unwise and injudicious expenditure.

Van Horne in reference to this scheme-an opinion which could have been obtained by hon. gentlemen opposite as it is available for them :
The Canadian Pacific Railway, the Graud Trunk Pacific Railway, or any other all-Canadian route, will never voluntarily carry a carload of wheat by the all-railway route around the great lakes to an eastern Canadian port for shipment abroad, for the simple reason that it will never pay any road to do so. That opinion is given in unequivocal language. Every person who reads it knows exactly what it means. Van Horne before their eyes. of Canada, a gentleman who has done a great deal to solve the transportation problem in his own province, the province of Manitoba, a gentleman whose services in the solution of the transportation problem have been very highly appreciated by the people of Manitoba, a gentleman who is the railway commissioner of that province, and a gentleman who more than any other man in the province of Manitoba has a right to speak for the people of that province. Mr. Roblin says:
I am willing to say, as railroad commissioner of Manitoba, representing, as I think I do, the majority of the people of Manitoba, that there has not yet dawned upon any of us, any use or practical benefit so far as we are able to see in this line, as proposed by Sir Wilfrid I.aurier, other than what any other road would give, in as far as the laying down of its line across our province is concerned.

There is nothing that I have been able to see in the project that will inspire us with the hope that it is going to secure for the people of Manitoba any practical or material benefit, other than what any other fine would confer.
